stem: Which statement defines one radian?

options.content: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the diameter
options.rationale: An arc equal to the diameter subtends 2 rad.

options.content: One three-hundred-and-sixtieth of a complete turn
options.rationale: That is one degree.

options.content: The angle turned through by a point on a wheel in one second
options.rationale: That describes an angular speed, not a unit of angle.

explanation: θ = s/r; when s = r, θ = 1 rad (about 57.3°).

stem: What is $120^\circ$ in radians?

options.rationale: This multiplies by 180/π instead of π/180.
This divides 120 by 180 but forgets the factor π.
This is 60° in radians.

explanation: $120 \times \dfrac{\pi}{180} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3} = 2.09\ \text{rad}$.

stem: What is the unit of angular speed in SI base units?

options.rationale: This is the unit of linear speed, v = rω.
Correct: the radian is a ratio of two lengths, so rad s⁻¹ reduces to s⁻¹.
This is the unit of acceleration.
This is the unit of the period, the reciprocal of what is needed.

explanation: ω = Δθ/Δt; θ = s/r is dimensionless, so ω has the base unit s⁻¹ (written rad s⁻¹).

stem: Points P and Q are on a rotating disc; Q is twice as far from the axis as P. Which statement is correct?

options.content: Q has twice the angular speed and twice the linear speed of P.
options.rationale: Every point of a rigid body turns through the same angle in the same time.

options.content: They have the same linear speed; Q has half the angular speed of P.
options.rationale: Q travels a larger circle in the same time, so it moves faster.

options.content: They have the same angular speed; Q has twice the linear speed of P.
options.rationale: Correct: ω is shared by the rigid disc and v = rω.

options.content: They have the same angular speed and the same linear speed.
options.rationale: v = rω, so the point further out moves faster.

explanation: All points of a rigid rotating body have the same period and ω; linear speed is proportional to radius.
hints: Do both points complete a turn in the same time?

stem: What is the angular speed of the minute hand of a clock?

options.rationale: This is the hour hand (one turn in 12 hours).
This is the second hand (one turn in 60 s).
Correct: one revolution (2π rad) per 3600 s.
This is the frequency in Hz; ω = 2πf.

explanation: $T = 60\ \text{min} = 3600\ \text{s}$; $\omega = 2\pi/T = 1.75 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.
hints: How long does the minute hand take for one turn, in seconds?

stem: A wheel of radius $0.40\ \text{m}$ turns through $1.5\ \text{rad}$. How far does a point on its rim move along its circular path?

options.rationale: This divides the radius by the angle.
This multiplies 1.5 by 2π × 0.40, treating 1.5 rad as 1.5 revolutions.
This converts 1.5 to radians as if it were in degrees.
Correct: s = rθ = 0.40 × 1.5.

explanation: $s = r\theta = 0.40 \times 1.5 = 0.60\ \text{m}$, with $\theta$ already in radians.

stem: An electric fan turns at a frequency of $5.0\ \text{Hz}$. Calculate its angular speed, in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.
explanation: $\omega = 2\pi f = 2\pi \times 5.0 = 31.4\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.

stem: The tip of a fan blade is $0.25\ \text{m}$ from the axis. The fan turns at $120\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. Calculate the speed of the tip, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
explanation: $v = r\omega = 0.25 \times 120 = 30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. There is no extra $2\pi$: ω is already in rad s⁻¹.
workedSolution: 1. $v = r\omega = 0.25 \times 120 = 30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. There is no extra $2\pi$: ω is already in rad s⁻¹.

stem: The rotor of a hammer mill used to grind maize turns at $2900$ revolutions per minute. The hammer tips are $0.22\ \text{m}$ from the axis. Calculate the speed of the hammer tips, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.
explanation:
1. $f = 2900/60 = 48.3\ \text{Hz}$.
2. $\omega = 2\pi f = 303.7\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.
3. $v = r\omega = 0.22 \times 303.7 = 66.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
4. Using the frequency instead of ω leaves out the factor $2\pi$.
workedSolution:
1. 1. $f = 2900/60 = 48.3\ \text{Hz}$.
2. $\omega = 2\pi f = 303.7\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$.
3. $v = r\omega = 0.22 \times 303.7 = 66.8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
4. Using the frequency instead of ω leaves out the factor $2\pi$.
hints: Convert rev/min to rev/s, then to rad/s.

stem: The Moon orbits the Earth in a circle of radius $3.84 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m}$ with a period of $27.3$ days. Calculate its orbital speed, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.
The wheels of a car, radius $0.32\ \text{m}$, turn at a steady $60\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$ without slipping. Calculate the distance the car travels in $5.0$ minutes, in m, to three significant figures.
explanation:
1. Speed $v = r\omega = 0.32 \times 60 = 19.2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
2. Time $= 5.0 \times 60 = 300\ \text{s}$.
3. Distance $= 19.2 \times 300 = 5.76 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m}$.
hints: Find the car's speed from v = rω.

stem: Through what angle, in radians, does the Earth turn about its axis in $7.0$ hours? Take the rotation period as $24$ hours. Give your answer to three significant figures.
explanation: $\theta = \omega t = \dfrac{2\pi}{24} \times 7.0 = 1.83\ \text{rad}$ (that is $105^\circ$).

stem: All points on a rigid rotating disc have the same linear speed.
explanation: False. They share the same angular speed, but linear speed v = rω increases with distance from the axis.

stem: Match each angle in degrees with its value in radians.
explanation: Multiply degrees by π/180.

stem: Complete the relationships for uniform circular motion.

payload.template: Angular speed ω equals 2π divided by the {{blank:a}}, or 2π multiplied by the {{blank:b}}. The linear speed of a point at radius r is r multiplied by {{blank:c}}.

explanation: ω = 2π/T = 2πf; v = rω.

stem: Give the SI unit of angular speed.
explanation: Angular speed is measured in **radians per second**, rad s⁻¹ (base unit s⁻¹).

stem: Define the radian.

points.description: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle…
…by an arc equal in length to the radius.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius of the circle.

explanation: Both "at the centre" and "arc equal to the radius" are needed.

stem: Show that the linear speed $v$ of an object moving in a circle of radius $r$ at angular speed $\omega$ is $v = r\omega$.

points.description: In one period $T$ the object travels the circumference $2\pi r$, so $v = \dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$.
So $v = r \times \dfrac{2\pi}{T} = r\omega$ (or: $s = r\theta$, divide by $t$).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In one period the object moves a distance $2\pi r$, so $v = 2\pi r/T$. One revolution is $2\pi$ radians, so $\omega = 2\pi/T$. Substituting gives $v = r\omega$.

explanation: Distance per revolution over time per revolution, then ω = 2π/T.
hints: How far does the object travel in one period?

stem: Nyasha times 10 revolutions of a slowly rotating turntable four times: $12.4$ s, $12.1$ s, $12.6$ s, $12.2$ s. A coin sits $15.0\ \text{cm}$ from the centre.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean period of the turntable, in s, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the angular speed, in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the speed of the coin, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Using half the range of the timings, calculate the percentage uncertainty in the angular speed, to two significant figures.
parts.explanation: Half-range $= 0.25\ \text{s}$; $\dfrac{0.25}{12.3} \times 100 = 2.0\%$. $\omega \propto 1/T$, so it has the same percentage uncertainty as $T$ (and as the time for 10 turns).
parts.workedSolution: 1. Half-range $= 0.25\ \text{s}$; $\dfrac{0.25}{12.3} \times 100 = 2.0\%$. $\omega \propto 1/T$, so it has the same percentage uncertainty as $T$ (and as the time for 10 turns).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why timing 10 revolutions rather than 1 improves the result, and suggest one further improvement.

points.description: Reaction-time uncertainty is the same for any timing, so it is a smaller fraction of a longer time.
Further improvement: time more revolutions (e.g. 20) / use a light gate or a marker and video / use a fiducial mark at the start-stop position.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The reaction-time error is roughly the same whatever is timed, so over 10 revolutions it is a much smaller percentage of the time. Timing 20 revolutions, or using a light gate with a flag on the turntable, would improve it further.

explanation: T from many revolutions; ω = 2π/T; v = rω; ω has the same percentage uncertainty as T.
hints: Divide the time for 10 revolutions by 10.

stem:
Small reflective markers are stuck to a spinning disc at different distances $r$ from its axis. A light-gate system measures the speed $v$ of each marker as it passes.

| $r\,/\,\text{m}$ | $v\,/\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ |
| --- | --- |
| 0.04 | 0.99 |
| 0.08 | 2.03 |
| 0.12 | 2.98 |
| 0.16 | 4.05 |
| 0.20 | 4.98 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the graph of v against r and state what it shows.

points.description: A straight line through the origin.
v is directly proportional to r, so every marker has the same angular speed (v = rω).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A straight line through the origin: v is proportional to r, as expected when all points share the same angular speed, v = rω.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Determine the angular speed of the disc from the gradient, in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the frequency of rotation, in Hz, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of revolutions per minute.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the angle, in radians, the disc turns through in $0.50\ \text{s}$.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Suggest why the readings near the axis are less reliable, and how the experiment could be improved.

points.description: Near the axis the speed (and the light-gate time difference) is small, so the percentage uncertainty in v is large / the marker's width is a larger fraction of its circular path.
Use smaller markers / more readings at larger radii / repeat and average each reading.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Close to the axis the markers move slowly and their width is a larger fraction of their path, so v has a larger percentage uncertainty. Use narrower markers, take more readings at larger radii and repeat each one.

explanation: v = rω, so v against r is a straight line through the origin with gradient ω.
hints: The gradient of v against r is ω.

stem: Explain why the radian has no dimensions, and why measuring angles in radians makes the equation s = rθ possible without extra factors.

points.description: θ = arc length ÷ radius: a ratio of two lengths (m ÷ m), so it has no unit.
By definition one radian corresponds to an arc of one radius, so the arc is simply r × θ (in degrees a factor π/180 would be needed).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: An angle in radians is defined as arc length divided by radius, a ratio of two lengths, so it has no dimensions. Because one radian corresponds to an arc equal to the radius, the arc for θ radians is simply rθ; in degrees the formula would need a factor of π/180.

explanation: The radian is defined as a ratio of lengths.
